title: Infosys Cleared in AI Worker's 'Sham' Contract Case in Australia
excerpt: Australia's Fair Work Commission ruled the AI expert's engagement was a standard three-way labour-hire arrangement, rejecting her claim that Infosys was her true employer.
body:
• Australia's Fair Work Commission dismissed an AI expert's unfair dismissal claim against Infosys.
  • She alleged a labour-hire arrangement was a "sham" contract masking her true employment by Infosys.
  • The Commission found it was a standard three-way labour-hire setup — and that Infosys was never her employer.
  • The ruling underscores how on-hire chains can create legal distance between host companies and dismissal claims.

An Australia-based AI expert has lost her unfair dismissal case against Infosys after the Fair Work Commission found that the IT services giant was never her employer — even though she worked on an Infosys project, carried an Infosys email address and used an Infosys laptop.

The worker, who is highly qualified in data science, process mining research, event log engineering and AI solution data engineering, argued that the labour-hire arrangement she was engaged through was a "sham" designed to disguise the employment relationship and let Infosys sidestep its employment obligations. She also claimed she had ultimately been forced to resign.

How the arrangement worked

According to the case record, the worker was approached on LinkedIn by an Infosys employee about a role contributing to a service management process transformation project for Optus. Because she was in Australia on a visa, Infosys could not employ her directly, so a third party was engaged to take her on as a subcontractor. After signing the contract, she received an Infosys email address and laptop and began work on the project.

She was later offered a full-time contract through a labour-hire firm that included a sponsored visa. Disagreements arose over who would pay the visa fees. She resigned in March 2025, giving two weeks' notice, and in an email raised concerns about what she called an "unfair" visa arrangement.

"I strongly believe it is important to stand up for my rights and advocate for workplace fairness, which is a fundamental value in Australian culture."

— The AI expert, in her resignation email

Why the claim failed

Infosys raised a threshold objection: it had never held any contract with the worker, so it could not have been her employer — and only an employer can dismiss someone. Without a dismissal, the Commission said, there was nothing to hear.

The Commission agreed. It found the setup was a standard three-way labour-hire arrangement, in which the employer is the labour-hire business, not the client the worker is placed with. The "real substance, practical reality and true nature" test the worker invoked — a provision in the Fair Work Act that asks decision-makers to look beyond contract labels — was about distinguishing employees from independent contractors, the Commission held; it does not allow a worker to treat the business she was placed with as her employer when the two never had a contract.

Searching for any agreement that might be implied from how everyone behaved, the Commission found none — noting that visa rules meant Infosys was never in a position to employ her in the first place.

What the ruling did not decide

The Commission was careful to spell out what it was not deciding. It made no findings on whether the arrangements between the various labour-hire and sponsoring companies were a sham, saying no such question arose in relation to Infosys. And because it found Infosys was not her employer, it never reached her separate claim that she had been pushed into resigning. The application was dismissed.

Why it matters for diaspora tech workers

The decision lands in a workforce reality many Indian professionals in Australia will recognize: highly skilled migrants, often on sponsored visas, routinely enter enterprise roles through chains of labour-hire firms and subcontractors rather than as direct employees. The ruling is a marker that those chains create real legal distance — recruiting a worker, handing over a laptop and approving timesheets did not, on their own, make the host company the employer for unfair dismissal purposes.

"Bringing skilled people in through on-hire chains can put real legal distance between a host business and unfair dismissal exposure — recruiting someone, handing them a laptop and approving their timesheets did not, on their own, make Infosys the employer."

— HRD Australia, employment law analysis

It is also a reminder that the much-cited "real substance" test has limits. It scrutinizes labels within an existing working relationship; it does not reassign who the employer is across a contractual chain.

What's next

The dismissal stands unless the worker appeals to the Federal Court. Broader scrutiny of sham contracting in Australia's tech sector is unlikely to slow: regulators and unions continue to probe arrangements where visa-dependent workers cycle through labour-hire chains with little of the security of direct employment. For Indian IT giants operating in Australia — Infosys among them — the ruling confirms the legal value of keeping on-hire engagements cleanly documented, even as it leaves the worker-side question of fairness unanswered.
nri_angle: The ruling carries weight for Indian tech professionals in Australia, many of whom work through labour-hire chains on sponsored visas — and now know host companies carry legal distance in dismissal claims.
